chapter.title: Basic Concepts
chapter.para: This chapter covers the ideas the rest of the book takes for granted: what the web is, how a browser and a server communicate over HTTP, and how CGI lets a program build a page on demand. It assumes no prior experience with any of them. A reader already familiar with the web, HTTP and CGI can go directly to .

section.title: Resources and Links
section.para: The web is a collection of resources connected to one another by links. A resourcewebresource can be a page of text, a picture, a piece of music, a video, or a file of any other kind. What makes these resources a web rather than a collection is that they point at each other.

A pointer from one resource to another is a hyperlink, or link. When you arehyperlinklinkhyperlinkbrowsing reading a page and a word or a picture takes you somewhere else when you act on it, you have followed a link. Following links in succession, from one resource to the next, is browsing the web, also called navigating it.

section.title: Resources Need Identifiers
section.para: Following a link requires a way to identify what it points at. Every resource therefore has an identifier, and because a link has to keep working over time and for everyone who follows it, that identifier must always designate the same resource.

Such an identifier is a URI, short for Uniform Resource Identifier. TheURIUniform Resource IdentifierURI Uniform part means that every identifier follows one agreed-upon syntax, so that the same form names a resource of any kind. http://example.com/photos/sunset.jpg is a URI. It identifies one particular resource, and any link pointing at that resource carries this identifier inside it.

Two related initials occur alongside URI. A URL, a UniformURLUniform Resource LocatorURL Resource Locator, is a URI that identifies a resource by stating where to find it; the example above is a URL, because it names a host and a path to reach. A URN, a UniformURNUniform Resource NameURN Resource Name, identifies a resource by name alone, saying nothing about where it is located. Both are URIs. The everyday web address is the URL kind, and it is the only one used here.

A URI names a resource, but the resource itself has to reside somewhere. It resides on a server: a program, running on some computer onserver the network, that holds resources and hands them out when they are requested. The terms resides on and is held are used here as if each resource were a file stored on that computer. That is the model to start from, and it is refined below.

section.title: The Browser and the Protocol
section.para: The resources you want to read are usually not on your own computer; they are on servers elsewhere on the network. A browser fetches them and displays them. When you request a URI, the browserbrowser locates the server named in it, asks that server for the resource, receives it, and presents it, for example as a page with its pictures in place.

The browser and the server need a common language to understand each other: a fixed set of rules for requesting a resource and for returning it. Such a set of rules is a protocol, and the one the web is built on isprotocolHTTPHyperText Transfer ProtocolHTTP HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. Every time you follow a link, your browser uses HTTP to request a resource from a server, and the server uses HTTP to answer.

What comes back is often a page, and a page is usually written in HTML, which describes its structure: thisHTMLCSSJavaScript is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link. The appearance of the page, its colours, spacing and fonts, is specified separately using CSS. Anything the page does on its own, such as reacting to input or changing as you read, is programmed in JavaScript. All the other resources travel alongside these pages: plain text files, images, sound, and the rest.

section.title: Static and Generated Resources
section.para: The earliest servers were pure servers in a literal sense. A resource was a file on the server's disk,serverpure and when a browser requested it, the server found that file and sent it back exactly as stored. A request for /photos/sunset.jpg returns the bytes of sunset.jpg. This is still the basic model of the web: a server answers a request by returning a resource.

Two limits follow from it. Some pages cannot be prepared in advance, because what they should say depends on something unknown until the request arrives: who is asking, the time of day, or the contents of a database that changes every minute. There are too many possible versions to store them all as files, and those versions do not stay fixed.

The second limit applies even when a page could be stored. Consider a site of forty thousand pages that share a common look: the same header, the same footer, the same colours and logo. When the company changes its branding, every one of those forty thousand files has to be edited to match. Editing them by hand is not practicable, and an incomplete edit leaves the site half in the old style and half in the new. Anything shared across many pages, such as the header, the footer and the styling, is better held in one place and applied to every page as it is sent.

Both limits point to the same requirement: a way to produce the resource on demand. Instead ofdynamic content returning a file prepared in advance, the server runs a program that builds the answer at the moment it is requested.
Several technologies do this. One of the oldest and most widely used is CGI.

section.title: The Common Gateway Interface
section.para: CGI, the Common Gateway Interface, is itself a protocol, in the sameCGICommon Gateway InterfaceCGI sense as above: an agreed-upon set of rules, in this case between a web server and a program. The rules state that when a request arrives for a certain URI, the server does not look for a file. It runs a program, and whatever that program produces is the answer. The program runs afresh on every request, and its task is to build the resource.

Two things have to happen for this to work. The server has to tell the program what it needs to know about the request, and the program has to return a complete answer. CGI defines both, using facilities every program already has.

The request comes in through the environment. When the server runs the program, it places the details of the request into the program's environment variables, the ordinaryenvironment variablesstandard input variables any program can read from the system it runs in. Which URI was requested, what kind of request it was, who is asking, what browser they are using, and dozens of other facts are each set as an environment variable with an agreed-upon name. If the request carries a body of data, as it does when someone submits a form, that body is fed to the program through its standard input, the same input stream a program reads when reading from the keyboard.

The answer goes out through standard output. Whatever the program writes to its standard output, the same place astandard output program prints to when printing to the screen, becomes the response. The server takes that output and returns it to the browser as the answer to the request.

The answer cannot consist of the content alone. The browser needs to know what kind of thing it is receiving: an HTML page, a plain text file, or a picture. CGI requires the program to state this first. Before writing any of the content, the program writes a short header announcing the content's type,headercontent type then a blank line, and only then the content itself.
The smallest complete answer a CGI program can give is:

One header line names the type of what follows, a blank line marks the end of the headers, and the content follows. The header comes first because the browser has to be told what is coming before it arrives.

A CGI program therefore has the following shape. It starts. It reads the request from its environment variables, and from its standard input if there is a body. It determines what the answer should be. It writes a header stating what kind of answer it is. It writes the answer. It stops. On the next request, the sequence runs again from the beginning.

CGI is language-neutral. Nothing in the protocol mentions any particular programming language. Environment variables,CGIlanguage-neutral standard input, standard output, and writing a few lines of text are available in every programming language. A CGI program can therefore be written in any of them, which is one reason CGI has remained in use: it requires almost nothing of the language it is written in.

CGI is not a fast protocol. A new program is started for every request, and starting a program has a cost. Under heavy load that cost accumulates, and other technologies avoid it. For most sites, such as a small business, a personal site or an internal tool, the cost is not significant, and CGI is simple to understand, simple to write, and behaves the same way everywhere.

section.title: From CGI to RexxHTTP
section.para: CGI still leaves a number of tasks to the program. You have to read the environment variables you need, by their exact agreed-upon names. You have to read and interpret the body on standard input. You have to write the header before the content, in the right form, with the blank line in the right place. None of this is difficult, but all of it is repeated in every program you write, and none of it is the work the program exists to do.
RexxHTTP handles that machinery: the environmentRexxHTTP variables, the standard input, the headers and their order. What you write is the part that decides what the answer should be.
